done.what: Every process started under a session's shell is reported by Windows itself: pid, parent pid, image path, command line, creation time, exit time, exit code, user and kernel CPU time. The shell is put in a job object tied to an I/O completion port; one thread for the whole program sleeps on the port. No hooks in the shell, no polling

A process is opened when it joins and held until its exit is recorded, so its pid cannot pass to another process meanwhile and its exit code and CPU time stay readable after it is gone. One that is already over when reached is checked against the session's job before anything is read, and still gives image path, parent, times and exit code; only its command line is lost. One that cannot be opened at all is recorded as seen, with its details left unknown

The job allows breakaway and kills nothing: a child that asks to leave (as the daemon launch does) still starts and outlives the session; a detached child that stays is still running after the session has ended and the job handle is closed; sensing works when PROTEUS is itself inside someone else's job; a program inside a session can still put its child in a job of its own (kill-on-close, a UI restriction), and that child and what it starts are still sensed

(review) The join race was being lost in practice and is now narrowed and repaired, though still not closed by construction. Found: only cmd is held at its start by the console host; a console program that starts a child without asking the console anything has that child running within 20 ms, and with every core busy the thread that creates the shell could be left waiting that long between creating it and joining it (a shell's first child was lost in 2 of 15 runs of the test suite; those runs had the review's extra session tests in them, which start more sessions at once, and the suite as delivered at 600b6d2 passed the 4 runs it was given). join_race.what: The shell is put in its job just after Windows creates it (portable-pty cannot start it suspended). A child started before that would never be seen.
join_race.as_shipped: the call that joins the shell to its job: p50 25-29 us, max 42-58 us (2 runs of 20 sessions). From the shell's creation time to joined: p50 3.4-3.9 ms, max 8.6-11.8 ms (28.8 ms once in the daemon), nearly all of it inside CreateProcess before the shell can run. The earliest a `cmd /c "cmd /c exit 7"` shell created its child: 30.3 ms after its own creation (p50 33.2 ms). First child seen in 20 of 20 sessions, twice
join_race.join_held_back_on_purpose: by 100, 1000 and 2500 ms: shell and first child seen in 5 of 5 sessions each. By 3500 and 5000 ms: 0 of 5 (the shell had finished before it was in the job)
join_race.why: The console host does not let a console program past its start-up until the terminal has answered the host's two opening questions (cursor position, device attributes) or 3 s have passed, and the session cannot send an answer before the join has returned: its threads are started after it. So the shell cannot run, let alone start anything, until it is in its job, for as long as the join takes less than 3 s. It takes about 30 us.
join_race.closed: No. The explanation above is true of cmd (a test, a_late_join_still_sees_the_shells_first_child, holds the join back 1 s and fails if that stops being so) and was wrongly taken to cover every console program: see measured.review.join_race and known_issues for what the review found and what was done.

known_issues: The join race is not closed by construction (review; this replaces the earlier wording, which said the console host closes it: that holds for cmd only). The shell joins its job about 30 us after CreateProcess returns, with the creating thread at time-critical priority so that it is not left waiting for a core in between, and anything the shell started first is gathered into the job afterwards. Still missed: a process the shell started that had already ended before the shell joined, if it left nothing running; and anything in a blocked (not merely preempted) creating thread's window that ended the same way. A stray gathered this way is recorded from the moment it is put in the job, with its true creation time. One that had asked to break away before the shell was in the job cannot be told from a stray and is gathered too (nothing is killed either way). Closing it for good means creating the shell inside the job (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST), which needs PROTEUS to call CreateProcess itself instead of through portable-pty.

Starting a session now takes one snapshot of the system's process list (the gathering above), on the thread that starts the session, after its priority has been given back: p50 7.6 ms, max 12.5 ms with 323 processes on this machine (50 snapshots). It is paid once per session, never while one runs. A cheaper listing (NtQuerySystemInformation) was not tried.

When a session's pseudo-terminal closes while its shell is still alive and stays alive, the end of the session is held back until the shell is gone or two seconds have passed (on the session's own thread; the window is not blocked).

A process started with CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB leaves the session's job and is not seen, nor is anything it starts. That is required (the daemon is started that way from inside a session). Processes created on the session's behalf by something else (a service, a COM server, a scheduled task, WMI) are not its descendants and are not seen either.

Command lines are journaled as plain text. A secret passed as an argument (`tool --password x`) is recorded, in the same file that already holds everything printed. Keyboard input is still never journaled.

If the sensor is later than a whole process's life and that pid has already passed to another process of the same session, the first process is recorded with the second's details and its exit is recorded late and without a code. The check that what was opened is in the session's job cannot tell the two apart. Not seen in any run; at the measured latency (hundreds of microseconds against lives of 20 ms) it needs the sensor's thread to be held up a hundred-fold.
The command line of a process that is over before the sensor reaches it cannot be read (measured: 0 of 2128; the sensor's thread runs at time-critical priority to keep it so). Its other details can.

The window's handler (app.rs: UiEvent::Proc into State.procs) is compiled but has never run: this lane may not open a window. The path up to it is tested (term.rs). `--bench` was not run for the same reason, so typing latency with sensing is unmeasured; the headless flood figure above is the only throughput check.
A process still running when its session ends stays 'running' in that session's ledger: its later exit is not recorded anywhere.

`proteus procs` reads the journal file. For a live daemon session the newest events can be up to a quarter of a second late (the daemon's flush interval), and reading time grows with the number of records in the journal (not measured on a large one).
CPU time comes from Windows in 15.6 ms steps: a short process shows 0, 15 or 31 ms.
Closing a session still ends only the shell (as before); there is no 'end everything this session started' yet, though the job makes it one call.

Under cmd.exe, `proteus procs > file` writes nothing to the file: the program is a windowed one that borrows the console, and cmd does not hand such programs its redirected handles. True of every proteus subcommand before this lane. A pipe from PowerShell, or any caller that passes handles explicitly, works.

The unit tests of the ledger (procs.rs), of the frame reader (remote.rs), of history marking (term.rs) and most of the World view's layout tests (world_tests.rs) run on events and ledgers written out in the test, not on recordings: pid reuse, a lost exit and a daemon from a later build cannot be produced on demand. The sensor's tests, the daemon's and those reading forge/samples are real processes and real journals. Said here because the rule is 'nothing mock'; the person merging should decide whether constructed inputs to pure functions fall under it.

`cargo test` run under cargo is itself inside cargo's job, which forbids breakaway: a test shell that is not yet in its session's job gets 'Access is denied' when it asks to break away. That is how the lost join was first seen (a_child_that_asks_to_leave_the_job_still_starts_and_outlives_the_session failing once in 7 runs).

An exit whose code reads 259 ('still running') while the process is not yet gone is put aside and re-read on a 1 ms timer until it is, for up to 2 s. Measured 7 times in 2128 exits, longest 2.5 ms; 7 is also the number of `cmd /c exit 259` among them (one per run of 300), so no ordinary exit was seen to need it.

Close the join race by construction: create the shell already inside the job (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST), which needs PROTEUS to call CreateProcess itself rather than through portable-pty; or have the host process sit in a job of its own so that everything it creates is born in one. Until then the race is narrowed (priority) and repaired (gathering), not closed

Review: a process the shell started before it was in its job is put in the job even if it had asked to break away (the two cannot be told apart at that point). Nothing is killed on its account today; whoever adds 'end everything this session started' (TerminateJobObject) must know that such a process would be ended with the rest.

Review: the measurements and the hunt for flaky tests loaded this machine: several bursts of 16 busy threads for 10 to 30 s each, and about 130 full runs of the test suite (7 s each, about twenty sessions at a time).

The socket generation is now 3. After this ships, a new window starts its own daemon; sessions living in a generation-2 daemon stay with their existing windows and are not offered to new ones. That daemon leaves by itself 30 s after its last session ends.
